body.statement:
There is a constant \(c_{\mathrm{lower}}>0\), depending only on
\(d,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L,e_0\), such that throughout \(n\epsilon\ge1\),
\[
 R_{n,\epsilon}^{\mathrm{DP}}
 \ge c_{\mathrm{lower}}\{R_n^{\mathrm{NP}}\vee\rho_G\vee\rho_F\}.
\]
The \(\rho_G\) term is witnessed by a localized one-record subexperiment.
For the \(\rho_F\) term, whenever \(\rho_F\ge\rho_G\), there are smooth
shared-sign two-fiber mixtures in \(\mathcal M_H\), separated by
\(\delta\asymp\rho_F\), whose prior-predictive samples admit a coupling with
expected Hamming distance at most
\(C\delta n^2h^d\ell^d\), where
\(h\asymp\delta^{1/\gamma}\),
\(\ell\asymp\delta^{1/q}\), and \(n\ell^d\le C\).  If
\(\rho_F<\rho_G\), the \(\rho_F\) lower bound is already implied by the
\(\rho_G\) branch.
body.justification: A same-class converse determines whether dense occupancy creates a new privacy radius or merely activates the first-order branch.
body.gap: Kennedy et al. give only the nonprivate term, and Acharya et al. give generic coupling inequalities rather than the occupancy-indexed causal mixtures needed for the two privacy terms.
body.consumer: It prevents an upper mechanism from being certified against a surrogate regression class or only a sparse diagnostic family.
body.proof_tex:
We prove the three lower bounds separately.  Constants denoted by \(c,C\)
below depend only on \(d,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L,e_0\), and may change from
line to line.

First, privacy cannot improve nonprivate risk.  Given any private Markov
kernel \(T\), define its conditional barycenter
\(\bar T(D_n)=\int t\,T(dt\mid D_n)\).  Since the output is in \([-2,2]\),
\(\bar T\) is a measurable nonprivate estimator with the same range.  By
conditional Jensen,
\[
 |\bar T(D_n)-\theta(P)|
 \le\int|t-\theta(P)|\,T(dt\mid D_n).
\]
Taking expectations, then the supremum over \(P\in\mathcal M_H\), and
finally the infimum over private \(T\), gives
\(R_{n,\epsilon}^{\mathrm{DP}}\ge R_n^{\mathrm{NP}}\).

For the dense branch, choose a nonnegative \(C^\infty\) bump \(g\), supported
on the unit cube and equal to one at the origin.  For a separation
\(0<\delta\le\delta_0\), put
\(h=c_0\delta^{1/\gamma}\) and
\(g_h(x)=g((x-x_0)/h)\), with \(c_0,\delta_0\) small enough that the support
lies in \([0,1]^d\) by the interior condition on \(x_0\).  Consider two laws
with uniform \(X\), independent \(A\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\),
\(\mu_0=0\), and \(\tau_0=0\), \(\tau_1=\delta g_h\).  Conditional on
\((X,A)\), take \(Y\in\{-1,1\}\) with mean \(\mu_A\), and construct
potential outcomes with these means independently of \(A\) given \(X\),
then impose consistency.  Scaling of the bump gives
\(\|\tau_1\|_{\mathcal H^\gamma}\le L\); all other Hölder conditions and
overlap hold, so both laws lie in \(\mathcal M_H\).  Their target separation
is \(\delta\).  A direct calculation on the two atoms of \(Y\) gives
\[
 d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P_0,P_1)
 \le C\delta\int\mathbf 1\{g_h(x)\ne0\}\,dx
 \le C\delta h^d.
\]
Couple \(X\) and \(A\) identically and draw the two binary outcomes from a
common uniform random variable; their conditional mismatch probability is
the absolute difference of their Bernoulli success probabilities.
Coordinatewise repetition therefore couples the product laws with expected
Hamming distance \(D\le Cn\delta h^d\).  Apply
\(\mathrm{lem:private-le-cam-coupling}\) with privacy slack zero.  For
\(\delta=c_1(n\epsilon)^{-1/(1+d/\gamma)}=c_1\rho_G\), choose \(c_1\) so
that \(10\epsilon D\le1\).  Thresholding any estimator at the midpoint of
the two target values turns it into a test, and on a testing error its
absolute estimation loss is at least \(\delta/2\).  The cited testing bound
therefore gives risk at least \(c\delta\).  If this choice exceeds
\(\delta_0\), use the fixed separation \(\delta_0\); since \(\rho_G\le1\),
decreasing the final constant gives the bound for all \(n\epsilon\ge1\).

We next construct the sparse two-fiber experiment.  The details are included
because exact one-record cancellation is essential for the claimed exponent.
Let \(G_h=g_h^2\).  Start with a fixed nonnegative smooth function
\(\eta\), positive on \([-1/2,1/2]^d\) and supported on \([-1,1]^d\).
For the lattice of mesh \(\ell\), normalize its translates by
\[
 w_j(x)=\frac{\eta((x-z_j)/\ell)}
 {\{\sum_m\eta((x-z_m)/\ell)^2\}^{1/2}}.
\]
The denominator is bounded away from zero, only a dimension-dependent
number of terms overlap, and \(\sum_jw_j^2=1\).  Thus
\(\phi_j=g_hw_j\) satisfies
\[
 \sum_j\phi_j(x)^2=G_h(x),\qquad
 \|\phi_j\|_{\mathcal H^s}\le C\ell^{-s}\quad(s>0),
\]
and only \(k\asymp h^d/\ell^d\) functions meet the support of \(g_h\).
For independent Rademacher signs \(\lambda_j\), put
\(f_\lambda=\sum_j\lambda_j\phi_j\).  Then
\[
 \mathbb E_\lambda f_\lambda(x)=0,\qquad
 \mathbb E_\lambda f_\lambda(x)^2=G_h(x).
\]
Take \(a=c_2\ell^\alpha\), \(b=c_2\ell^\beta\), and
\(\delta=4ab\), and choose \(h\asymp\delta^{1/\gamma}\).  Because
\(q=\alpha+\beta<\gamma\), one has
\(\ell\asymp\delta^{1/q}\le h\) after decreasing \(c_2,\delta_0\).

It is convenient here to take \(Y\in\{0,1\}\), still a subset of its
declared support.  If \(\alpha\ge\beta\), define the first fiber by
\[
 \pi_{P,\lambda}=\tfrac12,\quad
 \mu_{0,P,\lambda}=\tfrac12+b f_\lambda-\tfrac12\delta G_h,
 \quad \tau_{P,\lambda}=\delta G_h,
\]
and the second by
\[
 \pi_{Q,\lambda}=\tfrac12+a f_\lambda,\quad
 \mu_{0,Q,\lambda}=\tfrac12+b f_\lambda,
 \quad \tau_{Q,\lambda}=0.
\]
If \(\beta>\alpha\), instead use
\[
 \pi_{P,\lambda}=\pi_{Q,\lambda}=\tfrac12+a f_\lambda,\quad
 \mu_{0,P,\lambda}=\tfrac12-\tfrac12\delta G_h,\quad
 \tau_{P,\lambda}=\delta G_h,
\]
and
\[
 \mu_{0,Q,\lambda}=\tfrac12+b f_\lambda,\qquad
 \tau_{Q,\lambda}=0.
\]
The scaling bounds above show respectively that the propensity, control
regression, and effect have Hölder norms bounded by \(L\).  Smallness of
\(c_2\) places every propensity and conditional mean in \([1/4,3/4]\), so
the overlap condition follows from \(e_0\le1/4\).  As in the dense
construction, conditionally independent potential outcomes give
exchangeability and consistency.  Hence every component law belongs to
\(\mathcal M_H\).  Every first-fiber law has target \(\delta\), whereas every
second-fiber law has target zero.

We verify the cancellation.  Write \(s=2A-1\) and \(z=2Y-1\).  In the case
\(\alpha\ge\beta\), the four conditional masses, multiplied by four, are
\[
 p_\lambda=1+2zb f_\lambda+sz\delta G_h,\qquad
 q_\lambda=1+2sa f_\lambda+2zb f_\lambda+4szab f_\lambda^2.
\]
In the case \(\beta>\alpha\), they are
\[
 p_\lambda=1+2sa f_\lambda+sz\delta G_h+2za\delta f_\lambda G_h,
 \qquad
 q_\lambda=1+2sa f_\lambda+2zb f_\lambda+4szab f_\lambda^2.
\]
The two displayed moment identities and \(\delta=4ab\) show in either case
that \(\mathbb E_\lambda p_\lambda=\mathbb E_\lambda q_\lambda\) for every
\((x,s,z)\).  Thus the one-record prior predictives agree exactly.

For completeness, we bound the cost when signs are reused.  Conditional on
the covariates, join indices whose active \(\phi_j\)'s share a sign.  The
overlap degree of the underlying lattice is bounded in terms of \(d\), and
different connected components use independent signs.  For a component of
size \(m\), expand the products of the preceding four-atom masses and average
each sign.  Constant and one-record terms cancel by the preceding identity.
Every remaining term that differs between the fibers contains either one
factor \(\delta\), a product \(ab=\delta/4\), or two copies of the nuisance
amplitude absent from one fiber.  That absent amplitude is \(a\) when
\(\alpha\ge\beta\), and \(b\) when \(\beta>\alpha\); respectively
\(a^2\le ab\) and \(b^2\le ab\).  Summing the product expansion therefore
gives the explicit component bound
\[
 d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\overline P_m,\overline Q_m)
 \le C\delta (m)_2(1+c_2)^m. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, choose the first two record positions carrying one of the listed
factors in at most \((m)_2\) ways; the absolute sum over every remaining
position is bounded by the binomial expansion \((1+c_2)^m\).  Averaging
Rademacher monomials and summing the four atoms cannot increase this absolute
bound.  This proves (1), rather than assuming a collision property as part of
the construction.

For each component, put the pointwise minimum of its two finite probability
masses on the diagonal and couple the residual masses arbitrarily.  The
failure probability is exactly the component total variation in (1); on
failure replace all of its records, so the Hamming cost is at most \(m\).
If \(M_i\) is one plus the
number of other covariates within a fixed multiple of \(\ell\) of \(X_i\),
(1) and bounded overlap imply
\[
 \mathbb E[d_{\mathrm{Ham}}\mid X_1,\ldots,X_n]
 \le C\delta\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1\{X_i\in\operatorname{supp}(g_h)\}
 \mathbf 1\{M_i\ge2\}M_i^2(1+c_2)^{M_i}.
\]
Under the uniform design, conditional on \(X_i\), \(M_i-1\) is dominated
by \(\operatorname{Bin}(n-1,C\ell^d)\).  When \(n\ell^d\le1\), its
exponentially weighted moments are bounded and
\[
 \mathbb E[\mathbf 1\{M_i\ge2\}M_i^2(1+c_2)^{M_i}\mid X_i]
 \le Cn\ell^d.
\]
Also \(\Pr\{X_i\in\operatorname{supp}(g_h)\}\le Ch^d\).  We have therefore
constructed a coupling of the two prior-predictive samples with
\[
 D\le C\delta n^2h^d\ell^d
 =C n^2\delta^{,1+d/\gamma+d/q}. \tag{2}
\]

Now suppose \(\rho_F\ge\rho_G\).  The uncapped radii apply because
\(n\epsilon\ge1\), and
\[
 \rho_F^{D_F}=(n^2\epsilon)^{-1},\qquad
 \rho_G^{1+d/\gamma}=(n\epsilon)^{-1}.
\]
If \(n\rho_F^{d/q}>1\), then
\[
 \rho_F^{1+d/\gamma}
 =\frac{\rho_F^{D_F}}{\rho_F^{d/q}}
 <\frac{1}{n\epsilon}=\rho_G^{1+d/\gamma},
\]
contradicting \(\rho_F\ge\rho_G\).  Hence the sparse condition required in
(2) holds after the harmless fixed rescaling used to define \(\ell\).  Set
\(\delta=c_3\rho_F\).  Equation (2) gives
\[
 \epsilon D\le C\epsilon n^2\delta^{D_F}=Cc_3^{D_F}.
\]
Choose \(c_3\) so this is at most a fixed small constant and apply
\(\mathrm{lem:private-le-cam-coupling}\) to the two convex hulls.  Midpoint
thresholding again converts estimation to testing and gives risk at least
\(c\delta=c\rho_F\).  If \(\rho_F<\rho_G\), the already proved
\(c\rho_G\) lower bound implies the \(\rho_F\) bound.  Fixed-separation
versions handle the finitely many scale choices above \(\delta_0\), exactly
as in the dense branch.

We have shown lower bounds by fixed positive multiples of each of
\(R_n^{\mathrm{NP}},\rho_G,\rho_F\).  Taking the smallest of the three
constants proves their maximum lower bound and the theorem.
